utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Petersen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, it feels like we've been here for a while. I just have a few more questions for you this morning. You testified that the VJ wanted civilians to stay in Kosovo, not leave Kosovo, because their presence made it more difficult for NATO to hit military targets; right? Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall saying that.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: So your understanding at the time was that NATO was trying to avoid civilians; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assumed that it was trying to avoid that. Nevertheless, quite a number of errors were made. As you know, three refugee columns of Kosovo Albanians were mistakenly targeted by the air-strikes; one in the Meja area; one in Bistrazin village in the general surroundings, that is, along the Djakovica-Prizren road; one in the Korisa village general area in the centre of Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. So although there were some mistakes, your general understanding was that the intent of NATO was to try to avoid civilians; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I assume that's fair.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And because of that reason, the more civilians that were around, the more difficult it would be for them to hit military targets; is that the basis of the analysis that you gave us the other day?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We who worked in the VJ, specifically those of us work in the Pristina Corps, were never in favour of the idea that civilians should be expelled. We saw no reason for that. Secondly, by being left alone in Kosovo-Metohija, any movement by civilians would make it very difficult for our forces to move about. We could not longer move our own forces about. As was sometimes the case later on --

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Just one second. I think we may have a misunderstandings, sir. I'm seeking about what you told us the other day that the army -- it didn't make sense for the army to want the civilians to leave because it actually made it more difficult for NATO to bomb when the civilians were there. So I'm just asking you about the underlying rationale for that. And I'm asking you if the idea behind that is that when an area is densely populated and NATO has to try to avoid that civilian population, that then makes it more difficult for them to hit military targets; is that the basic underlying idea of what you told us the other day?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. For as long as there were inhabited villages and towns in Kosovo and Metohija, there was always population moving about. The security conditions were quite complex. Nevertheless, the citizens needed to move about and travel all the roads there between smaller villages and settlements and major towns. Had it not been for the public transport using those roads and civilians moving along, anything at all along that road would have been a target for NATO because NATO would have known that the only people possibly moving down that road were soldiers and the VJ, making any of them legitimate targets in their eyes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. So the presence of civilians and the need for NATO to avoid those civilians in some ways made it more difficult for NATO to bomb VJ military targets; is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that was the case, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you talked yesterday, I guess it wasn't yesterday at this point, you -- probably it was on Tuesday, you talked about the Supreme Command staff having a proclamation printed that was to try to keep Albanians in the area and that they tried to have this printed in the Albanian news. Do you recall discussing that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: And that proclamation ultimately was not printed; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was. It just wasn't published. The Albanian media refused to publish it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Okay. And I meant -- by printing, I meant publishing. So this -- this proclamation was never published or distributed in any way?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ever since 1981 because of the illegal education system, the young did not follow the official curriculum of the government of the Republic of Serbia. They were taught in Albanian alone. Therefore, for that proclamation to be accepted by the Albanian people at large, it was necessary for it to be published in Albanian in order to make it intelligible to all. Had it been accomplished in Serbian, it would have been intelligible to no more than a handful of Kosovo Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Well, my basic question is in Albanian or whatever language it needed to be distributed in, this was ultimately not distributed; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Efforts were made at the time, at least that's what I was told. As for later on, I have no idea whether it was eventually distributed or published or not. It's possible that it was published at a later stage, it's just that I don't know of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: You personally weren't involved in those efforts to distribute it, it was something that you heard about from others?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had the media centre, the ground floor of the Grand Hotel. Writers, journalists, as well as those from the BBC and some local agencies were there. I was personally approached by some of those journalists telling me the Albanian media were refusing to publish that declaration of the Supreme Command staff. That is the source of my information.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, sir. So let's look at that proclamation.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I believe it's D180. If we could have that on the screen. And we can just have the first page in e-court in English and in B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Now, if we look at this first paragraph, it says: "The evil monsters of the allied, American, Canadian, British, Dutch, Belgian, Italian, French, German, and Spanish have lashed out fiercely at the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. In their ruthless strikes, they do not choose their targets, they do not spare the holy places which are the pride of our civilisation. They bomb monasteries, churches, and mosques; even graveyards are not sacred to them. They wish only one thing, to subjugate us and to do us harm. In their onslaughts they are directing most of their missiles at cities and villages throughout Kosovo and Metohija." So, sir, this language about the not choosing targets, directing missiles at cities and villages, implying that these are indiscriminate strikes, you would agree that that was false; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Madam Prosecutor, the specific phrasing in paragraph one of this document, well, as far as that is concerned, I will agree with you that it is an example of exceptionally poor phrasing, in terms of inviting people or encouraging people to stay in their homes. That is an unfortunate turn of phrase. As to your question, whether there were any random attacks, or, rather, let me put it this way: Had I been the one writing this or phrasing this, I would have put it quite differently. I would try to phrase it more realistically and in a way that was more acceptable to the potential addressees of this proclamation. As for random attacks in Kosovo, as in Serbia, generally speaking, as you know, random attacks were carried out, bridges were targeted, as well as kindergartens. You probably know about all of that. There were a great number of civilian casualties, both in Kosovo and in Serbia as a whole. That is what they mean when they say poorly selected targets, that means targeting something that can never be a legitimate military target.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Well, I think in this proclamation it says in their onslaughts they are directing most of the missiles at cities and villages throughout Kosovo and Metohija. They do not spare Albanians or Serbs, Montenegrins, Turks, Muslims, Goranci, Roma, Egyptians, or anyone. So this isn't talking about random strikes; this is insinuating in no uncertain terms that the NATO bombs are directed at regular people. And based on what we were just discussing, sir, you yourself had said that that was not the intent of NATO. My question to you is: This is more propaganda than truth; would you agree with that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree that this document, and I've had a chance to look at it, as a whole reeks of propaganda. Nevertheless, to some extent, it also realistically reflects the situation as it was. Therefore, Madam Prosecutor, may I ask you this: Have you ever wondered about the victims in Meja, or some of them at least? You are saying, perhaps for good reason, that some of them came to grieve as a result of inhumane treatment and violations of International Humanitarian Law; were these, perhaps, the columns passing through Meja bombed by NATO? I myself have had an opportunity to see horrific images from Bistrazin, Meja, and Korisa when Albanian refugees started leaving Kosovo. Let me ask you a hypothetical question, if I just may. Do you believe that --

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, sir, we need to stick with me asking you the questions here today. And my question to you is just this: This document is telling people that NATO is directly targeting them. You have said, sir, that NATO was, your understanding, was that NATO was attempting to avoid civilians, which is why it was better to have civilians around. This document is not true; correct? That's my only question for you.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer shifts between your statement and my previous answer. Madam Prosecutor, Kosovo and Metohija was the most miserable place to be on planet earth at that point in time. NATO was perhaps trying to avoid that as any normal and civilised army would have, nevertheless, the question we must ask ourselves is, in practical terms, to what extent were they successful in their efforts to avoid civilian casualties.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Sir, I asked you a precise question about this document, and I'm not sure if I'm going to get an answer from you on that. So I'll move on to my next question. Now, you told us in your testimony that the point of this proclamation was to try - let me see if I can get the exact quote here - you said at page 11759 that: "This proclamation would serve to make clear to the Albanian population that they should not leave their homes and that they are safe where they are and that they should stay in their homes." Now, you would agree, sir, that telling people that evil monsters are indiscriminately bombing and directing most of the missiles at cities and villages throughout Kosovo would likely do the opposite of that, would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I also agree with the impression that the latter portion of this document would create, and you are not showing it. You decide to dwell on this first statement. Nevertheless, the character of this document reflects a sincere invitation to the locals to stay, saying they had no reason to leave. If you wish to judge a document based on a single portion of that document, then I can hardly be expected to agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: Well, sir, you are correct that at the end of this document there is a request to the Albanians to return to their homes and their every-day work. But you would agree that before they ever get to that point if someone read this and believed it, they would be terrified; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Terrified, yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: All right. I don't have any more questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Petersen. Mr. Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's start with the last document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have page two of that document displayed, the very end of that document. Thank you. Could we please have that in the B/C/S as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, sir, could you please read out loud the last paragraph saying "Albanians" and then from there.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure. "Only life together without hatred and contempt leads to a happier future, a care-free childhood for our children, regardless of religion or ethnicity. Let us all together make an effort to restore peace to our native area. Return to your homes and your daily work. Do so today."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We see the date here as being the 7th of April, 1999. You say that you were in the general Pristina area throughout the air-strikes. Can you tell us what the targets were between the beginning of the air-strikes and the 7th of April specifically in Pristina because that's where you were at the time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite a number of targets. If you leave aside the military targets, the Ministry of the Interior in the very centre of Pristina was targeted too. Several of the neighbouring Albanian houses were destroyed. The main post office was targeted too, leading to a breakdown in all communication lines. During that particular attack, again, a number of Albanian homes were destroyed. The waterworks system was targeted. Grmija was targeted. The oil derivatives depot near the Orthodox cemetery was targeted. This was a full-scale disaster. There was a plume of smoke rising, and I don't think it ever dispersed before the war ended. The depots were there and the reservoirs, and there was a thick plume of smoke emanating from the scene. Colonel Milutin Filipovic was the garrison commander, and he kept all the records. He was the one reporting on everything that was going on. All of this made life in Pristina unbearable to anyone including the Albanian population there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. NATO was hitting civilian targets outside Kosovo and Metohija during the war in 1999; do you know anything about that? Leaving civilian casualties in the wake of these attacks?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I am aware of that. NATO spokesman Jamie Shea addressed the world media several times and termed this collateral damage. For example, the horrible atrocity at the bridge near Varvarin where some children were killed. The Gurgalica [phoen] bridge, for example, where a passenger train was targeted. All these were atrocious crimes. Bridges were destroyed in the main cities such as Novi Sad, and Belgrade's kindergartens were targeted. But there are records showing the figures, the number of civilian casualties and facilities that were destroyed during NATO air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember any civilian casualties on the road passing through Podujevo, specifically near the village of Luzane during the war in 1999?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, NATO's planes targeted the bridge itself near the village of Luzane along the Podujevo road. They targeted a bus carrying passengers belonging to a [indiscernible] company known as Nis Express. The bodies were charred, so I couldn't identify the bodies by the time I arrived. It was a horrific sight, blood curdling.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: About the commander of the Pristina Corps security, you told us at one point that he was not keeping you informed of his whereabouts; nevertheless, there is this unit securing the commander. Wouldn't they keep you up to date as to their movements and whereabouts?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The unit securing the Pristina Corps commander, this being one of the tasks of the military police would report to their own superior. The commander of the 52nd Military Police Battalion who would then, in turn, regularly brief my own assistant for security and staff affairs who was in charge of the military police. He was one of my two assistants. And then there were daily briefings where he would report to me to cover matters such as these.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Based on these reports, would you normally know what you needed to know about the whereabouts and movements of the Pristina Corps commanders, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not entirely since, as I said, the commander was not duty-bound to always stick to his plans. Normally monthly plans were drawn up for counter-intelligence and physical security of the corps commander. The corps commander then approves this monthly plan, and we are all expected to stick to it. Nevertheless, the commander may sometimes change the plan without necessarily consulting anyone, but then it is his responsibility to bear in terms of his physical safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: During the war, did the commander ever move around without being provided by military police security?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was never the case. Heavy security was always provided for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When we discussed the exchange of information in the security organ in the Pristina Corps -- well, my question is as follows: Did you receive information that concerned the security zone of the security organ of the Pristina Corps? Did you receive such information from Superior Commands from the security department of the 3rd Army, from the security administration, and from the security departments of other armies?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Information was conveyed vertically up the chain, and all information and territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia that was contained and in the territory of the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Army, information from all organs that concerned the situation in Kosovo and Metohija, all that information was conveyed to the security department, that is to say, to us in the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you briefly explain the following for us: What is the professional leadership of units of the military police? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll simplify this. As in the command of each and every unit, the heads of certain branches of the infantry, of the artillery, of armoured units, and then you have heads of certain departments, financial departments and so on and so forth, in a similar way, in the security department, you have an assistant for security issues who, with approval of the head, is involved in these matters, these heads that I have mentioned and the professional head are concerned. You have to monitor how plans and programmes for training are carried out. You have to monitor how units of the military police are staffed, since those units have A category soldiers. They had to carry out security checks because these soldiers have sensitive duties. Security for the commander is a sensitive duty. Then you have to provide MP units with special equipment against intercepting telephone calls, against sabotage; so it involves training units of the military police. That is what professional monitoring means.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yesterday a colleague showed you a letter from the security department of the Pristina Corps. In the example of the letter sent from the communication centre, could there be a signature?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: A personal signature?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's clarify something. Investigation, I think, is the term; we spent quite a bit of time on it yesterday; the security department of the Pristina Corps in. Which part of a pre-criminal procedure is it involved?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the law, the Criminal Code, criminal procedure, it's involved in the activities prior to the crime -- prior to the criminal procedure. That is investigation, securing the crime scene, gathering the necessary material, evidence, and you have to make sure that the criminal does not move away, that he is arrested, that he does not flee.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Does this also involve detecting crimes and perpetrators and then taking certain measures in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It concerns gathering all information that might shed light on the crime in question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well. The work you were involved in, all the people who did sabotage with regard to the Army of Yugoslavia, were they the subjects of your work regardless of whether these were foreigners or locals?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says in the rules that regulate the work of the security department.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: For that reason, would you be interested if a mandate is abused in the members of the Kosovo Verification Mission, or rather, in members of non-governmental organisations and humanitarian organisations, journalists too?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I may clarify this. We weren't just interested in members of the Kosovo Verification Mission. They had a UN mission, so we weren't interested in them. We were interested in the activities of terrorists. When investigating terrorist activities, we were conducting legitimate activities; it was a legitimate threat for the units. When investigating terrorist activities, we obtained information that indicated that concern representatives of the Verification Mission were involved - you have shown a number of such documents to that effect. So we weren't really interested in Kosovo Verification Mission; that wasn't the focus of our interest, but it became involved in the matter, we became interested in them because they were involved with those that we were actually interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you told us what the duties of the security organ of the Army of Yugoslavia were, but I'm interested in the following: When you find out that there has been a crime, the perpetrator of a crime against the JNA, to whom do you file -- against the Army of Yugoslavia, to whom do you file a crime report?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We do that to the Prosecutor of the relevant military Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And then who launches the criminal procedure?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The court that is competence, that has jurisdiction, does that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: At whose request?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the request of the prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And then the procedure is further -- the further procedure is dealt with by the court organs? Can you get involved in that once a criminal procedure has been instigated?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the law of criminal procedure that was in force at the time, it was possible to do that until the time that the Prosecution took over the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well. If military policemen discovered anyone involved in a crime, would they prevent the person from committing the crime in the course of that act?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be his legal duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Would they then surrender this person to the relevant organs if the military organs weren't responsible for dealing with those individuals?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well. Yesterday we spoke about what certain houses of Albanians looked like. I'm interested in the following: The houses of Albanians in the village, Albanians of Muslim faith, could you describe the houses of those Albanians of Muslim faith?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. In my childhood and later, I often stayed with Albanian families as their guest. The vast majority of the rural areas in Kosovo and Metohija have typical Albanian houses surrounded by high walls. They have very large yards. And in the middle of those yards, there were these constructions in an oriental style, sort of castle-like constructions with openings. This was for the traditional vendetta idea that you had, but these houses were never built independently. It was part of a complex of a number of houses that were surrounded by a wall of a tribe or a family, as they say, because often, after there had been a marriage, brothers wouldn't separate the property. They all remained living in the same place together. They would build houses next to each other, and these houses would be surrounded by high walls.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What were these walls made of and what was the height of these walls?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually these walls were made of large concrete blocks, and the height varied between a metre and a half and two metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well. Yesterday my learned friend asked you some questions about the arrest or the attempt to arrest Adem Jashari. Was Adem Jashari asked to surrender to the security organs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, the witness has told us he wasn't there. How can you expect him to know the answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, he answered a number of questions from the Prosecution yesterday. He said he wasn't present, he wasn't there, but he had information, some information. So I'm asking him about that in relation to what the Prosecution asked him about. I'm asking him about the information he has about the subject he was examined about by the Prosecution. I wouldn't have put this question to him if he hadn't answered the Prosecution's questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Prosecution was asking about topics other than ones that involved direct personal knowledge. Your question here is wanting his direct personal knowledge. If you are wanting to ask him did he have reports about this and what did they say, we would allow you. But you are asking him was there a warning, or words to that effect. So if your questions are directed to what he knows from his reports, you can go ahead on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. The witness said that he didn't have any information about that. The army units weren't involved, he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, when mobilisation is carried out, is there a difference between the active and reserve forces in the units of the Army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When mobilisation is ongoing, no difference is made between active and mobilised force. At the time in question, they were all members of the active forces, and they have identical rights and duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, in response to some Prosecution questions, you said that you were in Djakovica when Prascevic was killed. How long did you stay in Djakovica on that day?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there for an hour and a half or two at the most. As I said, I already had other obligations so I apologised to the family, but I just went to visit them to express my condolences. I wasn't at Mr. Prascevic's funeral.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you about the following: You said that in the yard on a bench --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether I can mention the name of the person in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I wouldn't think there's any difficulty. He gave evidence. It's what's the subject of the question that can be the problem, not the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Nike Peraj was, therefore, present on that day when you went to express your condolences. Did you speak to Nike Peraj?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Like all the others who had come to express their condolences, he was sitting on the Bench. I was a bit surprised, given that it was a state of war, he was exposed, and I was afraid because of the relationship he had. I thought that some might notice this and inform the terrorists. However, he was having a small glass of rakija, and he was sincere. He had associated with Mr. Prascevic earlier on. And he told me that, not Mr. Prascevic, so I assumed that it was because of the fact that they were close that he felt it was necessary for him to appear there and to express his condolences.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether there were any conversations with Mr. Nike Peraj on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. There were quite a lot of people, relatives, who were there. So apart from greeting him out of courtesy, no, no, there were no discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday my colleague showed you paragraph 59 and 60 of a witness statement, of Peraj's witness statement, and she said, or reference was made to your meeting at the funeral and also to conversations referred to in paragraphs 59 and 60 of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we could see Exhibit P313, and could we have a look at paragraphs 59 and 60 of that exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 59, second line, where was the meeting held according to the witness's statement?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the witness says that it was in a private house in Djakovica in the vicinity of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And he then mentions who was present apart from yourself. In paragraph 60, what is said with regard to the meeting? What kind of a meeting was it? It's in the first line.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In paragraph 60 it says that the meeting I'm referring to was an informal discussion in a group that had met for completely different reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see P338 now. It's the journal of the 52nd Battalion of the military police. I'm interested in page 6 in the English version, and it's page 9 in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you the following: Did you arrive with part of the unit of the 52nd MP Battalion that was resubordinated to the 125th Motorised Brigade, or rather, that became part of the 125th Military Police Company of this brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the two platoons?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they had previously been subordinated to the 125th Company of the Military Police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have a look at page 13 in the Serbian version and page 10 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you see the entry for the 21st here? And item 2, line 3, towards the end, what sort of shift took over in the 125th Motorised Brigade? What kind of change occurred?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This company was visited by Gavrilovic, Captain 1st Class from the Battalion. So this is the company that was attached to the 125th. It wasn't a company, two platoons - but you signify that this is the fact by saying a company minus one - in the area of the village of Junik. This was done for -- in order to provide logistical support and on so forth as it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And who was replaced? What does it say at the end?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Stankovic, Jovica was replaced. As -- due to the combat around Karelj Kosovo [phoen], he had a nervous breakdown. And Captain Antic, Sasa or Sasa Antic, replaced him as commander of those two platoons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's now have a look at the 13th page 13 in the B/C/S version and page 10 in the English version. Page 15 in the Serbian version and page 11 in the English version. I do apologise, my mistake. Could we see the entry for the 28th, please, of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Above the heading of "Logistical Support," the first line above that, preparations to replace men from the Military Police Company that were attached to the 125th Motorised Brigade were carried out. And the date?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 28th of April, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now, please -- 330A. Exhibit P330A. I'd like to have a look at paragraph 46.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What is that exhibit, please, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's a statement of Witness K-73 that you have there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P00330A. Or perhaps it's dash A. P00330-A. We have already seen this exhibit; we saw it a few days ago. Could we see page 10. Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Could you please read the last sentence of this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean 45?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In Korenica, we got on a civilian bus and went back to Junik."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us if K-73 was in a unit there, and which one when he was involved in the operation in the Caragoj valley?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a member of Captain Antic's unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Was that unit getting ready to be replaced in relation to the 28th of April, 1999? You remember the replacement that we read about a while ago?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You said yesterday that you were not the responsible person nor indeed were you taking any measures in terms of finding out more about the circumstances surrounding Prascevic's murder. When you went there to express your condolences, did the family perhaps tell you anything about the circumstances of his death?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they just said he had been off to some sort of action and was ambushed on the way there and killed in the general area of such and such a village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: When police work is done by a police department anywhere in Serbia, what sort of clothes do officers normally wear in the line of duty?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, if they are trying to put a stop so some smuggling operation, the smuggling of weapons, for example, any other illegal actions taking place, as far as I know, most of the secretariats for the interior, their crime prevention departments, the officers would normally work in plain clothes. The nature of their job being to be planted in -- into certain environments where all these criminal offences were being committed, and still wanting to pass unnoticed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps know that back in the Ministry of the Interior they had introduced ranks?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the persons working for these crime police squads had ranks as a matter of fact?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well, thank you. Can you tell us about planning the Caragoj valley operation. Witness Nike Peraj, given his position in the 52nd Brigade, would have been involved in the planning of that operation, would he not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given his post establishment-wise in the 52 Artillery and Rocket Brigade, there was no way he could have been there, not even when the operations for that brigade were being planned, because the working methodology for the work for staffs and command envisages precisely what officers are there when a decision is made at one of these meetings. And this certainly wouldn't have applied to a case involving the forward command post since the distance in actually exercising a command is far greater than would have been the case in a brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What about paragraph 96, we spoke about that, from the witness Peraj's statement. I wanted to ask you whether the commander of the Pristina Corps back in 1999, General Lazarevic specifically, had an office Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What about the forward command post in Djakovica, the Pristina Corps forward command post, was there an operations centre there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. According to the instructions governing the work of commands and staffs, you normally have an operations centre only in operative units belonging to a brigade or in a corps. The first such unit would be the corps command. As for operative duty rosters in brigades and other lower ranking units, that is something that is organised. There was no operations centre at a forward command post. If you'd like me to, I can explain what exactly that implied. It was this whole system of communications of all the devices being used, the equipment for encrypting, and so on and so forth, all of that in a single room that was then used as an operations centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The statement goes on to say that there was a map made with see-through talcum on the wall where all of the details were recorded on this map regarding the operation in the Caragoj valley. What I would like to know is whether Nike Peraj was given access to this room allegedly holding -- housing this map showing all of the developments during the progress of the Caragoj valley?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I explained yesterday, there is no topographic map being used in any country in the world in any army in the world to cover an entire wall. The format is different, the size it different. There isn't an honest hard-working army command anywhere in the world that would display an operation plan like that for all to see over a whole wall. As I explained yesterday, the only thing that map was actually showing was the deployment of the army units, the border units, and the combat groups, as well as the locations of the Siptar terrorists in that area. This map was there throughout. As for Mr. Nike Peraj, I don't believe that he would have been allowed into that room at any point in time. I don't think he ever asked, let alone was actually granted permission. Certainly not to the forward command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Very well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djurdjic, you mentioned paragraph 96. Is that of this exhibit that is on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, this is Nike Peraj's statement, Your Honour. That's P313, paragraph 96, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise for not stating the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You told us yesterday that, after the war, you found out about the bodies in Batajnica. Did you know where those people had been killed, whose bodies were found at Batajnica?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you know anything about the circumstances of their deaths?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know anything about that either.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You were asked a question yesterday about the prosecution of brigade commanders for crimes committed during the war. Did you have any knowledge indicating that brigade commanders committed any crimes at all during the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a shred of information in 1998 or indeed 1999 indicating that brigade commanders were involved in the planning, organising, or, indeed, ordering and commission of any crime at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Had you known anything about that at all, had you had information indicating that, would the security service not have initiated proceedings against not just these brigade commanders, but, rather, any VJ officers, soldiers, at all?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the same practice that applied throughout peacetime, even for a far smaller infraction, people were replaced and dismissed, let alone brigade commanders, and let alone in the case of a crime. The corps commander would have had such a person dismissed on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Does that apply to all the other VJ officers too?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as I pointed out at, lower levels of command, there were those who were ordering for certain refugees to be singled out from the column in the 37th Brigade. And we submitted this information to all the other brigades as a practical example of what must not be done. There were lower-level officers, company commanders, and platoon commanders who, in certain situations, violated the provisions of International Humanitarian Law.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have P1543. Thank you. Specifically, page 10 of the English and page 2 of the B/C/S. The document on the right-hand side, could you please zoom in a little. No, that's the left document; I mean the one on the right. Yes, that one, thank you. The upper portion of that document, please. Just to make sure we got the English where we want it, I want the introduction to this document with the header in both documents in both languages. All the way up, thank you. Though I am looking at the English and it doesn't seem to correspond with the Serbian text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Petersen.

utterances.speaker: MS. PETERSEN
utterances.text: I may be able to assist with this. I think that what we see at the top of the page in English is actually the end of a different document that's being displayed in this. So I think that this document starts where it says "2 Pristina Corps Command." Does that look right, Mr. Djurdjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much indeed for your help. You are entirely right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, sir, if you look at the header, what exactly does it say?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pristina Corps Command, security section, to the Joint Command for KiM.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And there's a date underneath, right?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What about any filing numbers?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not a document as such, not the kind that was filed. It wasn't dispatched or addressed to any particular institution. As I explained yesterday, I typed up quite swiftly some information that I had in a rush and then forwarded this to Mr. Djakovic in order to keep ourselves mutually informed, as I explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P1329, please. My apologies, it must be P1328. The previous number is the number that I have, but I think it was quoted as 29 yesterday in the transcript and the error was all mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: General, sir, the OTP showed you this document yesterday, and what you told us about the header is that you could identify the filing number that was a reference to the Pristina Corps. What about paragraph 2 which reads "task" or "assignment"?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a textbook order for the Pristina Corps and then paragraph 2 details the tasks for the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please move down to paragraph 5 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: 5.1, sir, please focus on that. General, sir, which unit is it here that we see receiving a task?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 125th Motorised Brigade and then, in the brackets, the second battalion of the 58th Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to the task for this unit, is there any other task being assigned to any other unit under 5.1?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no task for any other unit. There were plenty of documents such as these, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you, you've explained that already. Let's try and save some time on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 11, please, if we can move down to paragraph 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 11, the first portion, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It talks about command and communications, that's what it says. You can see the command post of the Pristina Corps, its peacetime location. This clause is always there in each and every order relating to the Pristina Corps. The clause about the peacetime location, although, in fact, we abandoned our peacetime location before the beginning of the air-strikes. Nevertheless, for security reasons, we were never able to share with our subordinate commanders the exact location of the Pristina Corps Command. There were many units like that. Had any of those documents fallen into the hands of the terrorists, there was always the danger for NATO to bomb to bits the entire Pristina Corps Command. The subordinate commanders would normally receive scrambled communication. They would de-scramble it in order to find out the exact location at any given point in time of the Pristina Corps Command. Each time there was a document like this, the phrasing was always the same, talking about the command's peacetime location for the reasons I've enumerated.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Can you please move down to paragraph 13.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The speed at which questions and answers are proceeding is a little too fast, the interpreters are under too great a pressure.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best to slow down, and General, may you do the same, please, in order to make sure the job is done properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 13 is the first thing you can see there.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 13 talks about co-ordination with the MUP forces in terms of preparing and carrying out combat operations, meaning in a particular area. This is then to be organised before the commencement and during the actual progress or combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have D104 now, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Okay. An order entitled the Joint Command. We have a filing number, the one that relates to the Pristina Corps. What number is that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The filing number? 455-56.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Towards the bottom of the page, we see who the task is in relation to?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a textbook order by the Pristina Corps Command, so that's who it's in reference to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I think it's probably the next page in the English document where it says "Tasks." Could we please go to paragraph 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Sir, if you look at 5.1, which is the unit being assigned a task here?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tactical group of the 211th Armoured Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we flip on to the next page, please, to check paragraph 2. The previous page. 5.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Who is the task under 5.2 in reference to, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 5.2 - the document is being moved all the time; it's difficult to say. The 125th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: 5.3, what about that one?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 15th Armoured Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please move to the very last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Based on what's written there, who issued this order?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Pristina Corps Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: And what does it say at the end of the page?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Signed by Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Any signatures you can see on the face of this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none. Nevertheless, this was a signal, a hint to the units that this was something that had been co-ordinated and agreed upon with the staff, the MUP staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Who would have been in a position to amend this order in any shape or form?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only the commander of the Pristina Corps, the person who issued this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we move on to Exhibit 205, please. 105. D105.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: The right, could you please read the header, sir, what does it say, the filing number?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same filing number as in the previous order, 455-59/1.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: What about down the middle, what does it say?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Amendment to the decision on supporting the MUP forces in breaking up and destroying the Siptar terrorist forces in the area of Malo Kosovo near Podujevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please move on to the next page of this document, thank you. Rather, the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Who signed this document?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Pristina Corps commander, General Vladimir Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you were shown a portion of General Vasiljevic's transcript. You discussed that, particularly about that dinner, was he invited or not. Nevertheless, I would like to read back to you a portion from 5691 of the transcript in our own trial. General Vasiljevic says: "The two of us went to the Pristina Corps Command to that building, having exchanged greetings, General Pavkovic told me, Stick around, we shall be holding a meeting of the Joint Command." Tell me, were you standing next to General Vasiljevic as he was exchanging greetings with General Pavkovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there standing right next to him throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Did you hear Pavkovic tell General Vasiljevic that there would be a meeting of the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't see how he possibly could have. The greetings that were exchanged were a matter of pure protocol. It was a formal thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: You were then asked by my learned friend the following question. Please, I expect you to tell me, sir, I'm not jumping to any conclusions. Where exactly was General Vasiljevic seated, next to whom?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Next to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: How far from you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chair to chair, like that. You can imagine the distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: For example, had he had an open notebook right in front of him on that table, you would have seen that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: So did he, in fact, have an open notebook in front of him?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Much obliged. What about this room in which you were, how large was the table at which you were all seated?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was arranged in a semicircle, and it was no more than 2 metres across.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In which building were you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basement of the Grand Hotel, the information centre of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJURDJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you. Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well timed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, you were talking about the NATO spokesman, that he addressed the media several times and termed some actions as collateral damage. How did you learn about this address by the NATO spokesman?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was through conferences that were shown via the media in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You read it in Serbian media, in newspapers or wherever?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I listened to comments on the television. There were images from the press conference for NATO, and there were comments - I don't know English - but there were comments according to which he made statements to this effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You saw that on the television?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You mentioned the name of the NATO spokesperson. It was not recorded on the record this morning. Can you repeat the name?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, his name was Jamie Shea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You will be very pleased, I'm sure, to learn that that's the end of the questions for you. We would thank you for your attendance here in The Hague again and for the assistance you've been able to give. And you are free now to return to your normal activities. After we rise, a Court Officer will show you out. And we will adjourn now for the first break and resume at five minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: While the witness is being brought in, I should indicate that we need to finish this session earlier than usual at about 20 minutes past 12.00. So if you can bear that in mind as you plan the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please read aloud the affirmation shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Mr. Popovic has some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, before I commence with my examination-in-chief, since we both speak the same language, I would like to ask you to listen the question I put to you, make a brief pause, and then answer. And this will make it possible for the interpreters to do their work correctly. I would also like to ask you to speak slowly for the sake of the interpreters. Could you tell me your first and last name, please?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: My name is Milos Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When were you born and where?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: In 1951 in Miljenica [phoen] in the immediate vicinity of Valjevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, were you a member of the MUP, and, if so, up until when?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: I was a member of the MUP from 1984 up until the 30th of December, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you then retire?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 30th of December, at my personal request, I retired when -- I more or less took an early retirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, let's just repeat this for the sake of the transcript. You said when all the legal conditions had been fulfilled for retirement?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, all the legal conditions had been fulfilled, and at my request I retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Mr. Pantelic, what was your rank when you retired?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: I received a rank of colonel at the beginning of -- I apologise. At the beginning of 1999, I obtained the rank of colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you briefly tell us what duties you had in the MUP when you were employed there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: When I arrived in the Ministry of the Interior in 1984, I was the deputy chief of the municipality SUP. The organisation of the MUP was different then. It was one municipality, I was the deputy chief of the municipal MUP, and around 199 -- I was acting chief of public security. Then I was the chief of public security. Then I was the acting chief of SUP. And in 1991 I was appointed as the chief of SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Let's just clarify your answer. When you say that you were the chief of public security, within which body were you the chief of public security?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: When I say I was the chief, well, that was the position of the chief of public security. I was the chief of public security for the territory of six municipalities, Valjevo, Lajkovac, Ljig, Mionica, Osecina, and Ub. According to the organisation of the work at the time, there was that position - it no longer exists - but, at the time, it did exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This was necessary to make sure we knew what you meant when you said the chief of public security. Could you now tell us what duties you had to perform in 1998 and 1999 within the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: In 1998 and 1999 I performed the duties of the chief of secretariat. So all security problems in the territory of the secretariat, I had to deal with. That included these six municipalities, and those were the duties that I performed. I had to deal with the security for citizens, public order, crime prevention, and so on and so forth. So all security duties that were the responsibility of the MUP were my responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel is kindly asked to switch off his microphone when the witness is answering questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic. We'll go into details a little later. First of all, I'm now interested in the territory covered by your secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: It was the territory of six municipalities as I have said. Valjevo, Lajkovac, Ljig, Mionica, Osecina, and Ub. About 240.000 people live in that area now.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you could perhaps tell us the duties you had to perform as the chief of the secretariat.

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: My duties involved, above all, the system of organisation, commanding, control, co-ordinating work, issuing instructions, so all security issues that had to be dealt with in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Given the duties that you had, what was your responsibility as the chief of the secretariat?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: In the documents of the MUP or according to those document, I was responsible to the chief of the ministry for security in the Ministry of the Interior. Should I clarify this?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, at the time, there were a number of assistant ministers. I think there were four such assistants who were directly tied to the minister, but according to the regulations, I was responsible to the chief of public security. All of the four individuals had certain duties, and I remember what duties they had as far as professional duties are concerned and tasks. I had regular consultations with him. But with regard to other issues, it was the chief of the ministry for public security.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you have mentioned this, could you tell us who the four assistants were, the four assistants to the minister? And we'll talk about duties later.

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: If I don't count Vlastimir Djordjevic who was an acting chief for public security before and was appointed as assistant to the minister, from 1997 to 1998 the assistants were Radomir Markovic, later he became the chief of state security. So Radomir Markovic; Stojan Misic; Obrad Stevanovic; and Zekovic, I can't remember his first name. Petar Zekovic, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, do you know how they became assistants to the minister? Are you familiar with the procedure that has to be followed in order to become such an assistant?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm very familiar with the procedure. The government appoints such assistants at the recommendation of a minister. So our minister of the interior made such suggestions. I think that was in 1997; they were appointed in 1998. Prior to that period there were fewer assistants to the minister. However, they were appointed, and the minister divided up their duties. Each assistant was responsible for certain duties within the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, we'll deal with that when we speak about the relationships in the MUP. Let's just be more precise. When we refer to the minister, who are we referring to in this period of time?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: We are referring to the Minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic who, as far as I remember, appeared on the scene in 1997 and performed those duties until the year 2000 or 2001, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic. I'd like to show you some documents and ask you to comment on them. You have in front of you a binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence has prepared a binder for the witness. It has always proceeded in this manner to date. The binder has numbered documents. So, with your leave, we would like to use this binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, when I give you the document number, I'll tell you where you can find it, under which tab in the binder. We'll then have a look at the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first one that I would like to have on the screen is P66. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It's under number 1, tab 1, Mr. Pantelic, in your binder. Have a look at Article 7. Page 1. It says the minister prescribes the way in which ministry duties are to be performed and issues instructions for the way in which they were to be carried out. Can you comment on this article, and did the MUP in 1998 and 1999 function in accordance with this article?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: With regard to this Article 7, I think that it has -- it is derived from the Laws on Ministries and Government Administration; laws that were in force at the time. This just prescribes the way in which the MUP is to perform its duties. And instructions were issued for their execution. So the minister is responsible for all these issues in the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, could we please see document P357 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, it's on under tab 2 in your binder. We can see the document that is called "The Rules on the Internal Organisation of the MUP." Mr. Pantelic, are you familiar with this document, and does this document state how the MUP is to be organised in detail?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with the document. And I do remember the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll show you parts of this document so that you don't have to search your memory. Have a look at page 4 in the B/C/S version, first of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 3 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm interested in Article 3 which states the the following: For performing duties from Article 2 of the rules, the secretariat of the Internal Affairs will be responsible hereinafter secretariats, from areas that the ministry is responsible from, and its headquarters will be in the municipality of Ito [phoen]. And, under item 3 --

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it's Article 3 in the English. We can move on to the following page immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Item 3 refers to Valjevo for the municipalities of Valjevo, Lajkovac, Ljig, Mionica, Osecina, Ub? Is that what you said earlier on? Does that concern Article 3, item 3?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: Parts of the Ministry of the Interior had its territorial organisational units, and these were secretariats of the interior. Apart from its basic headquarters in the MUP, there were also territorial organisational units. There were 33 secretariats in the territory of Serbia, 19 of which were in the territory of central Serbia. And in the territory of Vojvodina, the Autonomous Region of Vojvodina, and in Kosovo and Metohija, there were seven secretariats each. So the MUP was organised in a territorial way as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can move on to Article 4 now. In secretariat, under Article 3, it says secretariats will be in Valjevo, there will be a detachment for Internal Affairs in Lajkovac, Ljig, Mionica, Osecina, and Ub. Could you briefly comment on what I have just read?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very briefly. We wanted to see what the secretariat of the interior would look like as territorial organisational units. The first thing that was taken into account was security, security issues, and the number of inhabitants in the territory of the municipalities concerned. Someone in the MUP would have a look at the situation, assess the situation, and decide that in the territory of my secretariat it was not necessary for me to have police stations that were lower organisational entity; but there would be these departments for Internal Affairs, and these departments were formed then in all five municipalities, Lajkovac, Ljig, Mionica, Osecina, and Ub. Departments for Internal Affairs were formed, and they performed all the duties that existed in the SUP and in the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's have a look at page 10 in the B/C/S version now and page 8 in the English version. It's Article 12 that I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Article 12, Mr. Pantelic. It says that secretariats carry out all the duties from the ministry, all the duties as determined by these rules, and they are responsible for the security situation in the territory that is their responsibility. Secretariats, in accordance with provisions of Article 7 to 11 of these rules, organise work and control of departments of intern affairs, that is to say, of police stations in municipalities. They are responsible for their work. Could you briefly comment on this article?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: A while ago I said that secretariats perform the duties that the responsibility of the ministry and the rules determine these duties. So all those duties and tasks that exist in the MUP and were performed by SUPs as well as by departments of Internal Affairs in municipalities, so there's a hierarchy, a system of organisation, but they practically did the same sort of duties. And this is in accordance with Article 12 of the rule book. What it says in paragraph 2 of Article 12 is that the chiefs of secretariats are responsible for their work, for the work of the entire secretariat of the Internal Affairs, and that includes these internal organisational units of the secretariats that were present in municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pantelic, could we have a look at Article 37, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 32 in the B/C/S version and page 31 in the English version. Article 37. I think in English we're looking at 27, whereas it should be 37. Page 31. Yes, that's right, that's the article. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, Article 37 says: "The following organisational units shall be established in the secretariats under Article 3 of these rules:" And then there is a list. Could you please tell us this, what about your secretariat? Did it have these organisational units? If so, could you comment in the briefest possible terms on the substance of this article?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's just like the rules say, that's exactly what the situation was in my secretariat. We had a total of eight departments, although in some secretariats they had lower level units such as departments. I had the crime police department. Its task being to look after the citizens' property as well as law and order. That was the priority. The next one was the police department. I'm sorry, I'm going back to the crime police department. There was general crime and temporary crime, shedding light on general crimes as well as explaining the circumstances about white collar crime. The police department had a police station and also inspectors in the department that were particularly in charge of special preparations, Special Police units, the reservists. In addition to all their other work, these were their priorities -- I mean their tasks. The next thing was the traffic police department. What we have there, the priority tasks were to check and regulate traffic as well as any administrative work having do with traffic, such as issuing drivers licences and that sort of thing. The next was the section for foreigners and administrative affairs. They were in charge of administering travel documents, any questions regarding the status of various persons, and so on and so forth. There was the fire prevention police section. They had sub-inspectors carrying out checks in terms of fire prevention across the six municipalities. It also had fire brigades, one in each of the municipalities. And they all answered to the fire prevention section. The next thing was the section for analysis records and information technology. This was a special section. I don't think this warrants any particular explanations. We know what they did. The communications section was maintaining communications at an appropriate level. And then the last thing was the department for joint tasks, and they had to do with personnel, with resources, equipment, finances, and other issues too.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please now go to Article 57 and Article 58. The relevant pages are 44 in the B/C/S and 43 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, Article 57 and Article 58. If you could focus on these, please. This is about the rights and obligations of the chief of the secretariat in addition to his tasks within the purview of a secretariat. These are lengthy; please read them and comment briefly. I just want to avoid having to read them myself.

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: Okay I'll read it for you, but the legibility is poor. "In addition to the tasks within the purview of the secretariats established by these rules in accordance with the law, the secretariat chief shall ensure and maintain co-operation with municipal town -- All right. "Ensure and maintain co-operation with municipal town and district organs, including provincial organs ..." I do apologise, but the legibility is really poor. I can't see what it says. "In performing" - I can't read this - "Internal Affairs, and it shall" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There's no point in the witness trying to struggle with what is on the screen. We have, as an exhibit, the original. We can read it. That will save you time.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. Thank you, thank you, Your Honour. It wasn't my intention to have the document read out loud; that was the witness's interpretation of my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you sir, just briefly comment on these two articles, if you could, Mr. Pantelic, we don't need to read them here. We have these in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
