utterances.text: We touched on these issues a minute ago. This is about the powers of the chief of the secretariat. The chief of the secretariat, in addition to all the security related tasks, co-ordination, control, organisation, directing, he also had certain responsibilities vis-à-vis the political structures, not just the municipalities where the secretariat was based, but also in all the neighboring municipalities as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Slow down your speech. The interpreters are working into several languages and they --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the president, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the microphone was off. Do you want me to explain this to the witness or perhaps you would like to run it past him again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I ask you to slow down your speech. The interpreters are working into several languages, and you are going too fast for the process. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I'll try to adopt the slowest pace possible. The chief of the secretariat established such political contacts, as were necessary, for example with the ... regarding Article 37, or rather, 57, the chief of the secretariat had to establish contacts with the appropriate social and political structures in the municipality. His responsibility, I think that was defined a while ago, we talked about it, and we reached the appropriate conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pantelic, within your own secretariat, did you have any reserve police forces and did you have Special Police units?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was certainly the case. We had some Special Police forces. They were organised in a particular way. We also had some reserve forces. They were organised in a similar way, but pursuant to decisions that came from the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'll be asking you a number of questions now about these particular members of your secretariat. First of all, I would like us to focus on the reserve forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For that purpose, could we please have P706.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: This is tab 3 for you, sir. P706. Thank you. This is a dispatch, the number is 587, sent by the assistant minister chief of the public security sector Colonel-General Vlastimir Djordjevic. Sir, if you look at paragraph 1 of this dispatch, or, rather, let me phrase it this way. My first question: SUP all 1 to 33 to the chief, what does that mean, and did this dispatch apply to the Republic of Serbia in its entirety?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: I explained a while ago that there were a total of 33 secretariats of the interior throughout Serbia, throughout the Republic of Serbia. The dispatch was sent to each and every one of those from 1 to 33. So, yes, that applies to the Republic of Serbia in its entirety. This dispatch followed an order by the minister of the interior. There is a reference here to that order by the minister of the interior who envisaged the use of the reserve forces. And what we see here is specific measures being ordered in terms of updating our lists and records. This was something that was an ongoing task with the secretariats and something that was being done all the time, because certain individuals were not quite ready for these tasks and then they would be replaced by other persons. Summons such as these were issued every 15 or 20 days in order to make sure how many men were there, how well prepared they were, what sort of equipment they had, their personal weapons. Additions were made to the resources of the unit, and some members were replaced occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P66, please. Page 3 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, this is the first exhibit that you saw, the Law on the Ministry of the Interior. That is tab 1 for you in your binder. Could you please look at number 1, please, page 3, Article 28, specifically. I do believe you are looking at the wrong document. Tab 1, which is the very first document in the binder in front of you, sir. That's right. Page 3, please, Article 28. It says: "The minister may call on members of the Ministry of the Interior's reserves forces to perform certain peacetime duties of the ministry." And then it goes on to state what these tasks or duties are. What about the previous order by the minister referred to in the person who produced the dispatch, does that somehow link up with the substance of Article 28?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: That is quite obvious. We have an article here telling you us how we should use the reserve forces in the ministry. And if you look at item 2, it was taken over directly from the Law on the Ministry of the Interior, specifically Article 28. It was based on these powers that the minister then --

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you very much, sir. We'll be getting to that at a later stage. My question was in relation to Article 28 of the law specifically, the one that I quoted to you. Article 28 talks about the powers of the minister in terms of using the reserve police forces; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is certainly right.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now could we please have D102.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: In your binder, sir, that is tab number 5. We saw the article of that law, and we also saw what Mr. Djordjevic invoked in his dispatch. What we have in front of us now is an order to call up and engage reserve forces, personnel, to carry out certain peacetime tasks of the ministry. This was signed by minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic. Could you please comment in the briefest possible terms and tell us how it relates to what you said previously?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: In the briefest possible terms, this order to call up and engage reserve forces is almost like an implementation of the previous one that we looked at. The minister was the only one with the power to do that, to call up these men. Based on that, he wrote this. And then the order simply specified what was to be done. The order specifically was about certain steps to be taken vis-à-vis certain issues, men who would be drafted normally for six-month periods; and then once that period expired, the minister would issue a new order in order to regulate the status of these members or men for the following period.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, could we please go to paragraph 2 of this order. It reads: "Secretariats of the interior shall engage reserve forces, personnel, in accordance with their own assessment, having obtained prior approval by the police administration of the ministry." Can you please comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'll try to use an example to illustrate this. For example, there is a security problem, for example, in my municipality. The territory covered by my secretariat. The first thing we do is to make an assessment of the security situation. If we are not able to cope with the tasks by using our regular police forces, we ask that these other forces be used, and we put in a request through the police administration of the Ministry of the Interior. So, following the assessment, a specific request was made to the police administration. I think they actually had departments there. There was a department for Special Police units, and there was a department for defence preparations. They would receive these requests, process them, and normally submit them to the minister for inspection or for review. The minister would then make a decision and perhaps approve use of those forces. And then the minister of the interior would go back to the original secretariat, in this case my secretariat, would inform the secretariat of the approval, and specify when the units would be arriving and what exactly the makeup of those units would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D103, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Before we go there, the date here was the 1st of July, 1998, in the previous document. Now, D103. That's tab 6 for you, sir. Mr. Pantelic, this is yet another order to call up and engage reserve force personnel, signed by minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic. You commented on that a while ago. So my question is: Is this order identical to the order that we were looking at a minute ago?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: These two orders are entirely identical except for paragraph 5; the dead-line is here extended from the 1st of January, 1999, to the 30th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Just very briefly, sir, based on Article 28 of the Law on Internal Affairs, that is what we see invoked here in this order, right? And that's what we were talking about a minute ago, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the article. The reference is to that article.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D101, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Tab 4 for you, sir. Instructions on the performance of Internal Affairs duties by reserve forces personnel of the ministry. First of all, I would like to ask you at the introduction, the first sentence, which reads "Pursuant to Article 7 of the Law on Internal Affairs," my question is: Is that the same article that we discussed at the beginning of your evidence today, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, this directive is based on Article 7 of the Law on Internal Affairs adopted by the minister himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What I'd like you to be focusing on now is Roman numeral I, basic provisions. Subparagraph 2. Don't read it, and I'm not going to be reading it back to you, just please skim it and comment on the substance, if you can.

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: It states in no uncertain terms what reserve forces may be used for. It says, In order to carry out certain peacetime tasks for the ministry, to prevent any activity undermining the security of the republic, or restore serious violations of law and order. This is about mass rallies. In the previous period, I believe, in 1998 and 1999, we had quite a number of rallies, demonstrations, staged and organised by the various opposition parties. So these units were to be used in such cases. Needless to say, they were also there to prevent accidents, deal with any natural disasters, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please move on to page 3, Roman numeral IV. Final provisions. Article 10. Article 10 reads: "The chief of the secretariat directs and co-ordinates work and is responsible for engaging reserve forces personnel in the area of the secretariat." Can you please briefly explain what exactly the article means?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: This is an example of very generic phrasing. The chief of the secretariat has precisely that job; he must direct and co-ordinate work. Specifically in relation to the reserve forces, the commanders of police stations would take over, inspectors working in police departments, all of these parts of the secretariat. And that normally happened at a local level, the level of local police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: We see that this was signed by minister Vlajko Stojiljkovic and the date is the 22nd of June, 1998. Mr. Pantelic, within your own secretariat, specifically 1998 and 1999, did you have any members of the reserve forces there?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just like any other secretariat in Serbia, I, too, had some members of reserve police forces under me. We tried to use them as seldom as possible due to financial problems; nevertheless, when Special Police units were in Kosovo and Metohija and when the manning levels were low across the police stations in the area, there were cases, not frequently though, where we had no choice but to use the reserve forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go back to P357 for a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Tab 2 in your binder, sir. Rules on internal organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 8, specifically, in the B/C/S. Page 7 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Article 6, please, if you could focus on that, sir. It says: "In addition to the organisational units envisaged in these rules, in order to perform tasks from paragraph 2 of these rules, the minister of the interior shall establish PJPs and Special Police Units, operative groups, and other special – posebne units as well." Mr. Pantelic, could you please just briefly comment and then we'll tackle this in more detail by using other documents further down the road.

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: It was first stated in the law and then in these rules, the minister has the right to set up PJPs and Special Police Units. The minister had sole power to set up such units, and their task was to carry out certain security related assignments.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P58, while we are still on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Tab 7 for you, Mr. Pantelic. This is a decision to set up Special Police Units. The first sentence reads: "Pursuant to Article 6 of the rules on the internal organisation of the Ministry of the Interior." Is that the article that we read a minute ago, sir? Is that what the reference is to?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you go to page 2, this was signed by minister Zoran Sokolovic, and the date is the 1st of August, 1993. Can you tell us about these Special Police units. When were they set up and what was their purpose, what were they to be used for, and did this apply throughout the Republic of Serbia covering its territory in its entirety?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: We see this decision to establish Special Police units, adopted by the then-minister Zoran Sokolovic back in 1993. In a way, if you look at Article 6 of the rules and the internal organisation of the ministry, Special Police units were formed or set up. There was a name change somewhere along that road, but nothing about the substance of these units changed. A total of 15 detachments were set up, police detachments, stationed in Belgrade, Novi Sad, Pristina, Uzice, Kragujevac, and Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, one thing I'm particularly interested in is article 2 of this decision, it reads --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please pause until the text is displayed on the screen so the interpreters can follow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course, I'll repeat this.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Article 2, paragraph 2. Placing at the ready the assembling and engaging Special Police units for the performance of such tasks as described in article 1, paragraph 1, of this article. This is done pursuant an order of the minister and approval by the minister and the chief of the public security sector. Can you please comment on that briefly?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, what I need to say is that this decision was adopted in 1993. From that day on, these units continued to operate, under a different name at one point, but nothing about the substance of their work or nature changed. The one thing that needs pointing out, and I believe that it is clearly demonstrated by paragraph 2, item 2, the assembling and engagement of PJPs for the performance of these tasks is something that is done pursuant to orders by the minister and possibly orders by the chief of the department, providing he was previously authorised by the minister to do that. Things are perfectly clear as far as these units are concerned; they could only ever operate having previously obtained approval from the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, were these units established for the territory of the -- for the entire territory of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think this decision is quite clear. All the secretariats in the territory of the Republic of Serbia, all 33 secretariats, had Special Police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were these regular police units, or were they police units that were engaged when necessary? Or if you could provide more details, perhaps you could explain the principle according to which they functioned, how they were organised.

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: Let me first answer the first part of your question. They were units that were formed to perform certain tasks or to deal with certain security issues. As I said previously, the minister decided about all these issues and they were engaged on the basis of security issues that prevailed in a given territory. These units were engaged when it was necessary. The question is who -- who engaged those units and where they were engaged from. Part of the answer to the question is in this decision on the formation of Special Police units. These members of the police force were in uniform. It was the active police force that included the regular police or the transport police, traffic police. And sometimes reserve forces were included too. They performed their regular duties and tasks within the secretariat and, when needed, when they were engaged - and we are dealing with ad hoc situations in this case - when needed, they would go to the territory of the secretariat where a certain security issues had arisen. They would be placed under the command of the secretariat staff in question or under the command of the chief of the secretariat, if there was no such staff. And when the security problem had been dealt with, they would then return to their usual positions in their secretariats in their respective secretariats.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's have a look at item 6 since we are dealing with this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the following page in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It says that: "Ministry employees and members of the Special Police units shall be deployed and perform their duties that they have when they are not engaged as part of the Special Police units, and they have the rights that their position gives them in accordance with the rules." So is that what you saying, that they were performing their regular duties, in fact, when they weren't engaged in Special Police units?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I have been discussing when they would return to the ministry. When a specific problem in another territory had been dealt with, they would then return to the positions, the positions that they held according to the rule book on the organisation of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You are talking about Special Police units in general. A little later on I'll ask you about 1998 and 1999. But since we are dealing with certain general facts, I'm above all interested in whether the Special Police units were used in what sort of circumstances before 1998 and 1999, or during 1998 and 1999, if that was ever the case?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: Special Police units were used a lot earlier, that is certain. I've already said we had a lot of political incidents, public incidents, a lot of demonstrations, public gatherings, expression of discontent on the part of the citizens; and in many such situations, members of the Special Police units would be used.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To clarify certain matters, within your secretariat did you have any members of the Special Police units; and, if so, how many such members were there within your secretariat? How many members of the Special Police forces, and how were they deployed, how were they trained?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: The secretariat for Internal Affairs in Valjevo gave three companies, provided three companies. At the beginning, there were four, but later, three, for the Special Police units. Workers of the secretariat were members of the 35th Detachment or the 65th Detachment and of the 85th Detachment of the Special Police Units. The headquarters of the detachment that they were sent to, that members of the secretariat in Valjevo were sent to, was in Uzice. I said that Valjevo gave one company for the A version, for the B version, and for the reserve forces. The company had about a hundred men, including three platoons and logistics. When they went to the detachment, they would report to the positions they had been called to; they no longer had duties -- or the secretariat no longer had the duty to monitor them. They were under the command of the detachment commander, or, rather, under the command of the staff that they went to.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. For the sake of the transcript, line 11, page 57, when they returned from certain tasks that they had been assigned to, for example, members of your secretariats, where did they return to?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: They returned to their own secretariats.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The translation was somewhat different in that line, that's why I put that question to you. When we are talking about general matters with regard to Special Police units -- well, tell me, when you referred to demonstrations, violence on the street in which members of the Special Police units were involved, for example in the territory of Serbia and Belgrade, when you sent a unit of your own into such areas, would they report to someone? If so, who did they report to, and, as of that point in time, who would be responsible for their acts?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: Once Special Police units had been sent in, regardless of the formation concern, once this had been done, the secretariat no longer had any duties. The SUP no longer had any duties, the secretariat that they worked in. So once they had left the territory of the secretariat of Internal Affairs, they were directly responsible to the commander, or, rather, to the command, to the staff or to the secretariat they had been sent to. They were directly responsible to them for their activities. That was the case if you would send in Special Police units to the secretariat in Novi Sad. In such a case, they would be placed under the command of the chief of the secretariat, or, rather, of the staff, if such a staff had been established to deal with the specific problem. I myself, as the chief of the secretariat, had no responsibility over them at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Pantelic, we'll return to that issue and go into details later. But first have a look at Exhibit P57. It's under tab 10 in your binder. Mr. Pantelic, this is a decision on forming a staff in the ministry for terrorism prevention. It's dated the 16th of June, 1998, signed by Vlajko Stojiljkovic, the minister. Above all, my question is: Were you aware of the fact that in June 1998 in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija there was a staff of the ministry for terrorist prevention, the prevention of terrorism, in fact?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, by all means. I was aware of the existence of this staff. I had to be aware of the location to which I was sending Special Police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My following question, in fact, had to do with that, when you referred to staffs that had authority that were responsible for Special Police units after they had been sent into the field from the secretariat -- well, could you tell me whether this staff that was formed pursuant to this decision, could you tell me whether this staff had authority over the Special Police units that you sent from your secretariat to the territory of Kosovo and Metohija in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: If one has a careful look at this decision, I think that everything is quite clear. The only body that was responsible for the organisation, for the acts, for the instructions to carry out certain tasks was the staff of the ministry in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll discuss the details later on when going through this decision. But, first of all, I have another question. Under item 1 we can see that certain individuals are named. It says the chief of the staff Major-General Sreten Lukic. Which party was he a member of?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: He was a member of the public security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then it says the deputy leader of the staff David Gajic. Which department, which sector in the Ministry of the Interior was he employed?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: David Gajic, I'm sure he worked in the state security sector. As to the position he held at the time, I couldn't say for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then it says the assistant head of the staff of special operations Milorad Lukovic. Which department did he work in?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: I know Mr. Lukovic personally. He was the deputy head of staff for special operations in the state security sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So we see that the members of this staff were members of the state and public security sectors. Who could have established staffs or any other bodies that were composed of members of both departments, and who was in a position to issue orders to them?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Interior in organisational terms is composed of two main elements: You have the department or sector for public security, and you have the department or sector for state security. The heads of those departments were directly related to the minister. So only the minister could take decisions with regard to those issues. The head of the public security sector couldn't issue orders of any kind to the head of the state security sector and vice-versa. So these were the two main organisational units that were related under the minister and his orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Have a look at the following page. Under Roman II it says -- it mentions the following: It says that the staff has the duty of planning, organising, and controlling the work of organisational units within the ministry and also to control the work of the attached units for terrorism suppression in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. Does item 2, in fact, relate to what you were saying about sending in Special Police units from your secretariat, sending them into Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: That's correct. The staff has to control the work and engaging of organisational units from the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. I apologise, do continue.

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: The task of the staff is to organise, direct, and plan the work of the Special Police units present in that territory. In addition, this decision means that SUPs from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija were placed under the command of the staff in Pristina. I think that this situation is clear, the main responsible body in the territory of the region of Kosovo and Metohija, at least in security terms, was the staff of the Ministry of the Interior. They are responsible for performing these tasks in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My last question before we have the break. If you have a look at Roman III, it says, For its work and the work in the staff and the security situation, that's parts of the staff's tasks, the head of the staff shall be responsible to the minister to whom he shall submit reports on the security events, measures taken, and the results of the measures taken. Could you briefly comment on what I have just read out.

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: What is important here --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are two types of comments. I'm not -- intervene before, but if the witness is going to comment on the meaning of it, separate and apart from what is written here, I think he should tell us what the basis of his knowledge is. If he is just going to read the document and tell us what it says, that's all fine; but if he is going to give an assessment, he should tell us the basis of his assessment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic, I have no idea what you're leading to. You do, but the point is that the witness cannot interpret the meaning of what is here. The witness may explain how it operates in his experience. You understand the distinction?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. We can then continue with this issue after the break, because I think you said that we had to finish or adjourn a little earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We must have the first break -- second break now, and we adjourn, resuming at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Could we have a look at Exhibit P133.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, it's under tab 8. Thank you, that's the document. Mr. Pantelic, we can see letter 1268 dated the 28th of July, 1998, my question is as follows: Who is this letter addressed to, and is it intended for the entire territory of the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: This letter was addressed to all secretariats of the interior in the territory of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please read out the first paragraph in this document, and in particular the second paragraph and tell me what it is about. And comment on the sentence, Send to the members of the Special Police units to the secretariat. And then do you see your detachment, or, rather, not your detachment but the detachment that members of your secretariat were within?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: Here it says to whom members of the Special Police units should be sent and to which places. The detachment that was part of my secretariat is the 65th Secretariat, and it's being sent into Kosovska Mitrovica. It's being sent there to assist and has been placed under the command of the staff in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If you have a look further on, please comment and say what it says about how they are to be sent into the territory, and what does it say about the transport and so on and so forth? What sort of a document is this, in fact?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: In this document, certain problems that concern engaging special police units in the territory of the Autonomous Region of Kosovo are being referred to. As I have said, it's a matter for the administration -- the police administration of the MUP. In accordance with the security assessment in Kosovo and in accordance with the instructions issued by the staff in Pristina, they have to order secretariats of Internal Affairs as territorial organisational units to prepare a certain number of men in companies that they are providing in centres where detachments are formed. Here it says what sort of measures have to be taken, what has to be prepared, usually such letters would mention the measures that have to be taken. It would mention what sort of equipment has to be taken, what sort of uniforms are to be worn. It would refer to lunch packets, logistics, per diems that were to be paid, and so on and so forth. So such letters were quite frequently drafted. There would be 30- or 40-day shifts. So every 40 days we would more or less receive a letter of this kind, a document of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: I'll just ask you to be very precise and to make a distinction between engaging and sending in. So is this a letter that is dealing with engaging units or sending them in, and could you tell us what the difference is? Who was responsible for engaging such units, and who was responsible for sending them in?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: As I have said, as far as engaging units is concerned, one knows how they would be engaged. It was through a decision from the minister that went through the Ministry of the Interior, and the secretariats, the local secretariats of Internal Affairs would send them in. I think there were 15 detachments, so it depended on how many members of the Special Police units were already in the territory of the Autonomous Region of Kosovo. And on that basis a decision would be taken to send in other units. So I, as the chief of the secretariat, would, in fact, send in units as instructed by the police administration within the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As to where a certain unit would be sent to, well, on what basis were such decisions taken?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: Such decisions were taken on the basis of assessments that the staff made in Pristina on the basis of the entire overall security assessment with regard to which territory was under threat of terrorist activity. It was on the basis of all security issues that were raised. The staff would then assess the situation. It would then contact the police administration. And that administration would then contact the staff in return and the secretariat of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's now have a look at P1184, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It's under tab 11 in your binder. Just a brief comment, please. Have a look at this letter dated the 14th of January, 1999. Item 2 refers to the 4th Company of the 83rd Detachment of the SUP in Valjevo -- of the 85th PJP Detachment in Valjevo. So is it the same case that is concerned, the same men being sent in?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: It's the same sort of letter, for all intents and purposes, certain forces from certain detachments are being engaged. 85th is in question, the detachment that employees from the Valjevo SUP were in. So we also have the variant with reserve forces. An order is being issued to prepare them, to send them in. It says where they should be sent in, which place, and what conditions. It says what should be prepared. So logistics is being prepared. I think this letter is more or less identical to the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pantelic. Tell me, from the time that members of the Special Police units were engaged and when they were sent in in accordance with the letters from your secretariat, instructions from your secretariat, from that point in time, what was your responsible as chief of the secretariat with regard to those units? I'm talking about the period 1998, 1999 specifically. I'm talking about the period that we referred to and in relation to the documents I have already shown you.

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: As soon as Special Police units were dispatched, I no longer had any responsibility vis-à-vis those units anymore. They would be placed under the command of the secretariat or staff to which they were being sent. They were no longer supposed to send back any reports to me. Sometimes, though, I would pick up the phone to ask questions, such as how they were doing, whether they needed any help from me, or anything like that. There was no reporting, though. And they were certainly under no obligation to send back any reports to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would, nevertheless, like to talk specifically about Kosovo and the situation there in 1998 and 1999. Primarily 1999. When you sent these Special Police units to Kosovo, under whose command were they? And as for reporting, what sort of information was being forwarded to you?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: Special formations of Special Police units such as companies would be dispatched on a periodical basis. They would spend 30 or 40 days there and then they would have a break. Nevertheless, the security situation was gradually becoming more and more complex in Kosovo and Metohija. So there were a number of problems that were occurring. And it was sometimes the case that these units would stay in the area nearly all the time. We've seen a number of dispatches following orders by the ministry. They would report to serve under the command of the Pristina staff. They would go to an area covered by a particular secretariat and report for duty there. The dispatch always defined clearly where they were to go and report. Nevertheless, the staff was the supreme body in terms of orders as far as the police in Kosovo and Metohija were concerned. They would normally issue specific orders, where to go, where to report to, what equipment to carry, and all the other logistical aspects of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: When they arrived and when they were placed under the command of the staff, as you said, what sort of information, if any, would you receive from them following their arrival?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: In practical terms, I received virtually nothing from them, no information. They were deployed in the area. Only when they were in a position to get in touch with me, would I communicate with senior officers, that is to say company commander, deputy company commander or perhaps detachment commander. The purpose being just to get some general information on their situation, how they were getting along, and whether there was anything I could do for them. The gist is no one was systematically forwarding any kind of information to me, the simple reason being I had no such authority at this time over them.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Were you receiving any information about anti-terrorist operations or indeed on the way the unit was being used in some operations throughout Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: There was no such information. We had the daily bulletin which we would receive on an almost daily basis. Sometime it didn't arrive. The information on terrorist operations was quite terse. There would normally be two or three sentences. This or that happened in such and such an area, leading to the following consequences, and then on like that. And that's where the reporting stopped as far as that was concerned. We had no information at all on any anti-terrorist operations with the exception of some men who were in the area, my own men, whom I would sometimes speak to over the phone just to check how they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned terrorist operations. You mean terrorist attacks on the security forces; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm talking about. I had the misfortune on the 26th of March, 1999, to see the following happen in a single day: Along the road between Lajkovac and Rezelaj [phoen] or, rather, as I was accessing the village, there was an ambush by the terrorists. Five people were killed and six seriously wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 65 ter Defence Exhibit 1149. Thank you. This is 4729 for the OTP 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: You have that at tab 11, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reference is K003-6325. That's the document, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, it's a dispatch. The number is 2917. The date is the 20th of March, 1999. Could you please go to the portion that relates to the Kosovska Mitrovica SUP. Could you go to paragraph 2, read it for yourself, and just briefly comment, please. Is this the sort of information that you would receive at the time in terms of anything that had to do with the Special Police units that were dispatched to Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: As for members of the Special Police units that were sent to Kosovo to perform security related tasks, I would receive official information via a dispatch, unless we were dealing with a serious injury or with a death among our ranks. This is a typical dispatch, it tells you exactly what happened, it specifies the area and the time. Following the terrorist attack and an attempt to track down and arrest the perpetrators, two police officers, members of the secretariat of the interior in Valjevo injured themselves. It was a case of self-inflicted injury.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour. May this be received, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D00782, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D007-0078. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, you'll find that at tab 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please immediately go to page 2 of this document. Chronologically speaking, it predates page 1. It's just the way the document was loaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: We see the dispatch date of the 27th of March, 1999, from Kosovska Mitrovica. It is addressed to you. And if you could please read this for yourself. The next page of that document, please. This is the dispatch that I'm talking about. If you could please briefly comment in relation to the members of your SUP who were killed there. Please, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: The Kosovska Mitrovica SUP or the crime police department in Mitrovica is here addressing the secretariat of the interior in Valjevo. There is an Official Note here drafted by members of the Mitrovica secretariat who were working with an investigating magistrate. They were at the crime scene. They established the situation as they found it and proceeded to describe it in their Official Note and this dispatch. As I said, they would only keep us informed of situations such as these and any related activities that they were undertaking. That also being the reason I received this particular dispatch at the time. That notwithstanding, I had been informed about this. I had received a phone call several hours earlier on. I had to do something about contacting the families of those wounded and kill. First, information would be forwarded by telephone and then later this would be followed by a dispatch from the relevant secretariat in Kosovo and Metohija or the Pristina staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at page 1 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, it's an Official Note produced by the Kosovska Mitrovica SUP. The kind of information that it deals with is the same as we have discussed; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, as I said a while ago, the crime police department put together this Official Note on the spot. They were going to use this as a stepping stone to further investigate this atrocious crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may this be received, please. One thing I'd like to point out is that the document contains more pages than I have shown the witness, since it also talks about some items that were found on the SUP men who were either wounded or killed, the men from the Valjevo SUP. I didn't see any need to go through all these documents, since I do not consider them to be documents of particular relevance to this trial. Nevertheless, I would like to have the document exhibited. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be received as D00783. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, another question about members of the PJP which were dispatched from your secretariat to Kosovo and Metohija. Did you ever tour the units there in 1999? If so, how many times?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: Throughout 1998 and 1999, I regularly visited my units there, except for the period of the aggression and air-strikes by NATO. During that time I didn’t go down there because Valjevo had been targeted on a number of occasions, a total of 21 times. Therefore, because of the precarious security situation, I was unable at that time to visit them in the area. I believe the last time I visited was sometime early in 1999. In 1998, I think I paid them at least three visits in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was the purpose or objective of those visits? What did you talk to them about?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: Many things were discussed, but the priority was as follows: We knew about their tasks; we knew about their patrol duties; we knew about the check-points and the work they performed there; we knew about what it meant to keep the area under control. Mostly, we discussed billeting conditions, their health, their mental health, just to make sure that there were no men having problems with that. Was the command happy, were the police officers happy. So that was the gist of most of our conversations there.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P708. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: You have that at tab 13, sir. Mr. Pantelic, the next set of documents that I'm about to show you comprises dispatches from the public security sector. In order to speed ourselves along through this, let's start with the first one. What sort of a dispatch is this? Does that apply to Serbia's territory in its entirety? And please briefly comment on the substance.

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: This was a dispatch that came to the secretariat, and the area it covered, three or four times a year. You can tell that a dispatch like this was sent to all the secretariats across the Republic of Serbia. In a way, this was a perfectly ordinary occurrence for us. This dispatch tells us something in relation to state holidays and religious holidays, saying we should step up our security measures in order to reduce any security problems or risks in our areas to a minimum. In practical terms, it tells us that we should step up our patrols and regular routine policing. It also says that other types of operative steps should be taken. It says we should try to ID more people and take other steps to prevent any negative things from happening, such as criminal offences. It also tells us to step up security measures in all areas of our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Is this something that is perfectly usual in the work of a sector such as yours?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is perfectly ordinary. And normally this would happen three or four times a year. I didn't even need to read dispatches such as this one since I knew by heart what they said already. The only thing that we would look into was whether there would be an active-duty or a passive-duty. Apart from that, these dispatches were always identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have Exhibit D234.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: That is tab 14, sir. The 18th of June, 1998. Another dispatch. Again did this apply throughout the Republic of Serbia? And the other question, Does it have to do with the routine tasks of the public security sector with the exception that here they are talking about diplomatic and consular representatives?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: This is a dispatch by the minister of the interior on a unified course of action to be taken vis-à-vis diplomatic staff and consular staff as well as members of international organisations and international humanitarian organisations. In this dispatch, the minister orders that all be treated in the same way and that vehicles be stopped. He says we should explain to these members of international organisations where exactly they are on their way to and what they could expect along the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Is this not a general overview of the sort of business and the sort of tasks performed by the public security sector?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, this unified course of action is here being ordered to keep any discrepancies from arising between the various municipality and to make it possible for people to move about Kosovo and to reach their destinations.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said this dispatch was by the minister of the interior. Was it customary for the minister of the interior to send out dispatches that had to do with the work of the public security sector?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: If you ask me, this one should have been dispatched by the department for foreigners in the border affairs section. This would have been within their purview and not the minister's. Nevertheless, probably because of the sheer importance of the matter, it ended up being the minister who actually signed this.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P1202, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Tab 15, sir. Again, a brief comment if you can, sir, please, about this dispatch. Does it apply to the Republic of Serbia in its entirety? Is there anything about the tasks performed by the public security sector? And briefly, quite generally, what it says.

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: Much the same as the previous one, this dispatch was addressed to all secretariat chiefs across the Republic of Serbia. It's about stepping up overall activities in every field, and it concerned the danger of the explosives being planted in important facilities - for the country's economy - along major roads, in buildings, housing estates, institutions, and such-like, the message being to step up our overall activities in a bid to keep the overall security situation under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. P1203 is our next document.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Tab 16, sir. Dispatch 1827. The date is the 7th of October, 1998. The preamble or paragraph 1 states that there is pressure being exerted on sovereignty and territorial integrity. That's what it says. Was this dispatch addressed to all, and is it not about measures to be taken by the operatives of the public security sector, particularly bearing in mind this introduction?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: Much the same as the previous one, this one was addressed to all the secretariats across the country. Again, they are being told to step up certain types of activity, virtually all of their activities, in order to tackle such problems as are mentioned in the body of the dispatch itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit D433.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Tab 17 for you, sir. It's a dispatch of the public security sector 451/98. The date being the 8th of October. It's about special provisions about measures to be taken in case of an armed attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see the following page, particularly the last paragraph on the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you briefly read for yourself and tell us what it's about, what the point is of this entire dispatch. Again, did it apply to the territory of Serbia in its entirety, and did it concern the public security sector?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: The same thing applies as to the previous dispatch. It concerns all of the secretariats throughout Serbia. It was produced in October 1998. There were huge problems in the market in terms of food supplies and oil derivatives. This became a hotbed of speculation because the market being what it was lent itself easily to practices such as that. The government was convened to pass and adopt a special package of measures. The decree was forwarded to us by the chief of the public security sector for our information and so that we were duly informed and able to take measures about it. If you look at paragraph 6, this is only an operationalisation of potentially devious behaviour. This is about concealing certain goods, selling certain goods, raising prices, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Pantelic. I have one more question before we conclude for the day. Dwelling on this document, this dispatch and the previous ones that I've been showing you. Is this regular business or routine business for the public security sector?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: In what sense? Would you care to clarify a little.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Is this routine daily business for the public security sector, steps that are normally taken to improve overall security in the country?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: In this specific dispatch, it specifies that these are special measures. That is to say that the decree says that these are special measures. These measures were being implemented on a permanent basis by the internal affairs organs. Nevertheless, this one instructs that particular attention be paid to these phenomena and events. One had to bear in mind the overall economic and political situation in the country, and this was a potential hotbed for deviant forms of behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Preventing speculative behaviour such as this, was this in itself something that the public security sector normally did?

utterances.speaker: MILOS PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was my understanding of my previous answer, and I'm telling you that was certainly the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Your Honours, I believe it is time for us to draw to a close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We must adjourn now, and we resume on Monday, I believe in the morning, at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
